publications.title: Pico: A Modular Framework for Hypothesis-Driven Small Language Model Research
publications.venue: EMNLP 2025 Systems Demonstration · Suzhou, China
publications.finding: A modular framework that lets you change one thing in a small language model's architecture or training and directly watch what it does.
publications.takeaway: Small-model research should be a science, not guesswork.
publications.summary: Building small and medium language models is still more art than science: tight parameter budgets make every design choice matter, yet researchers lack systematic ways to test and refine ideas. We introduce Pico, a lightweight, modular framework of two libraries that give researchers a sandbox for making targeted changes to a model's architecture or training procedures and directly observing the effect on its behaviour. To support reproducible experiments, we release a suite of baseline models, pico-decoder, trained under standardised conditions and open-sourced for the community. Case studies show how Pico supports iterative small-LM design and analysis.
publications.featured_finding: A modular framework for changing one part of a small model's architecture or training and measuring what that change does.

publications.title: BabyBabelLM: A Multilingual Benchmark of Developmentally Plausible Training Data
publications.venue: EACL 2026 (Main Conference) · Rabat, Morocco
publications.finding: A multilingual collection of datasets modelling the language a child hears from birth to fluency across 45 languages, with benchmarks and baseline models.
publications.takeaway: Developmental data has no business being English-only.
publications.summary: We built BabyBabelLM, a multilingual collection of datasets that model the language a person hears from birth until they acquire a native language. The collection curates developmentally plausible training data of roughly 100 million English word-equivalents across 45 languages. Alongside the data we create evaluation benchmarks and train baseline models. The aim is to support multilingual pretraining research and language acquisition studies.
publications.featured_finding: Developmentally plausible training data, about 100 million words per language, for 45 languages, with benchmarks and baseline models.

publications.title: Cross-Lingual Alignment Without Joint Training: Do Monolingual Language Models Converge on Universal Representations?
publications.venue: EMNLP 2026 Main Conference · Budapest, Hungary

publications.takeaway: If monolingual models converge on their own, the structure is in the languages, not the training.
publications.featured_finding: Asks whether language models trained separately on single languages converge on shared representations without any joint training.

publications.title: Less is More: Pre-Training Cross-Lingual Small-Scale Language Models with Cognitively-Plausible Curriculum Learning Strategies
publications.venue: CoNLL 2024 BabyLM Challenge (Paper Track) · Miami, Florida, USA (Nov 2024)
publications.finding: Curricula that follow real theories of child language acquisition, applied language by language, can beat non-curriculum baselines across four language families.
publications.takeaway: Copy how children actually learn, not just how much.
publications.summary: Curriculum learning is a popular way to make Small-Scale Language Models (SSLMs) more cognitively plausible in the BabyLM Challenge, but it has rarely improved much over non-curriculum models. We ask whether theories of linguistic acquisition can specify finer-grained curricula. We build age-ordered corpora of Child-Directed Speech for four typologically distant language families and implement acquisition-inspired curricula cross-lingually. Comparing three curricula that replicate the predictions of acquisition theories (Growing, Inwards and MMM) on a standard SSLM architecture, we find fine-grained, language-specific curricula can outperform non-curriculum baselines.

publications.title: ByteSpan: Information-Driven Subword Tokenisation
publications.venue: ICML 2025 Tokenization Workshop (TokShop) · Vancouver, Canada (August 2025)
publications.finding: ByteSpan builds a subword vocabulary by grouping bytes a language model finds predictable, giving vocabularies that align with morphology better than BPE for English.
publications.takeaway: Maybe tokenisers should learn morphology, not just compress.
publications.summary: Recent dynamic tokenisers work directly on bytes and pool their latent representations into patches, much like word-segmentation models that mark boundaries where an autoregressive model's prediction error spikes. We ask whether grouping predictable bytes, rather than pooling their representations, can yield a useful fixed subword vocabulary. ByteSpan is an information-driven subword tokeniser that uses an external byte-level LM during training to find contiguous predictable byte sequences and group them into subwords. It produces efficient vocabularies with higher morphological alignment scores than BPE for English, and shows similar compression and Rényi efficiency across 25 languages.
publications.featured_finding: Grouping bytes that a language model finds predictable yields subword vocabularies that align with morphology better than byte-pair encoding (BPE) for English.

publications.title: Measuring Grammatical Diversity from Small Corpora: Derivational Entropy Rates, Mean Length of Utterances, and Annotation Invariance
publications.venue: ACL 2025 Main Conference (Poster) · Vienna, Austria (August 2025)
publications.finding: New information-theoretic measures quantify grammatical diversity from small corpora, staying stable across syntactic annotation scheme and corpus size.
publications.takeaway: You don't need a huge corpus to measure grammatical richness.
publications.summary: We introduce information-theoretic measures, derivational entropy rates alongside mean length of utterance, for quantifying grammatical diversity from small corpora. We show the estimates stay robust to the choice of syntactic annotation scheme, a property we call annotation invariance. They also hold up under limited corpus size.

publications.title: Meta-Pretraining for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Named Entity Recognition in Low-Resource Philippine Languages
publications.venue: 5th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL), EMNLP 2025 · Suzhou, China
publications.finding: Adding meta-learning to the pretraining of small decoder models lets them transfer named-entity recognition zero-shot to Philippine languages unseen during training.
publications.takeaway: Teach small models to adapt and they travel to new languages.
publications.summary: Named-entity recognition in low-resource languages usually means finetuning very large multilingual LMs, which is often infeasible under memory or latency limits. We ask whether small decoder LMs can be pretrained so that they adapt quickly and transfer zero-shot to languages unseen during pretraining. To do this we replace part of the autoregressive objective with first-order model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), testing on Tagalog and Cebuano, which are typologically similar yet differ in their actor/non-actor voice systems. Across four model sizes (11M–570M), MAML lifts zero-shot micro-F1 by 2–6 points under head-only tuning and 1–3 points after full tuning, and cuts convergence time by up to 8%. Gains are largest for single-token person entities that co-occur with the Tagalog case particles si and ni.

publications.title: Teacher Demonstrations in a BabyLM’s Zone of Proximal Development for Contingent Multi-Turn Interaction
publications.venue: BabyLM Workshop, EMNLP 2025 · Suzhou, China
publications.finding: ContingentChat, a Teacher–Student framework, teaches a 100M-word BabyLM to hold more grammatical, cohesive back-and-forth conversation.
publications.takeaway: Tiny models can learn to actually hold a conversation.
publications.summary: Child–caregiver dialogue has a property called contingency: prompt, direct, meaningful exchanges between the speakers. We introduce ContingentChat, a Teacher–Student framework that benchmarks and improves multi-turn contingency in a BabyLM trained on 100M words. Using a new alignment dataset for post-training, the BabyLM produces responses that are more grammatical and cohesive. Adaptive Teacher decoding strategies give only limited further gains. The work shows targeted post-training helps dialogue quality, and frames contingency as a hard goal for BabyLMs.

publications.title: Looking to Learn: Token-wise Dynamic Gating for Low-Resource Vision-Language Modelling
publications.venue: BabyLM Workshop, EMNLP 2025 · Suzhou, China
publications.finding: A lightweight vision-language model with token-wise dynamic gating learns from very little data and leans on images for content words, language for function words.
publications.takeaway: The model learned when to look, nobody told it to.
publications.summary: Training vision-language models on cognitively plausible amounts of data means rethinking how models combine words and images. Within the Vision track of the BabyLM Challenge 2025, we propose a lightweight decoder architecture with token-wise dynamic gating for adaptive fusion of linguistic and visual cues, feature modulation and channel attention to stretch limited visual information, and auxiliary contrastive objectives for visual grounding. Across five benchmarks (BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Winoground and VQA) it matches or beats multimodal baselines. The dynamic gate also discovers interpretable patterns without supervision, favouring visual cues for content words and linguistic cues for function words.

publications.title: BLiSS: Evaluating Bilingual Learner Competence in Second Language Small Language Models
publications.venue: BabyLM Workshop, EMNLP 2025 · Suzhou, China
publications.finding: BLiSS is a benchmark of 1.5M minimal pairs built from real learner errors, testing how well second-language small models capture the systematic patterns of learner language.
publications.takeaway: Learner mistakes are data, not noise.
publications.summary: Cross-lingual extensions of the BabyLM Shared Task push Small Language Models to simulate a wider range of acquisition scenarios, including code-switching, simultaneous and successive bilingualism, and second language acquisition. Yet there is no benchmark for the formal competence of cognitively inspired models of L2 acquisition (L2LMs). We introduce the Benchmark of Learner Interlingual Syntactic Structure (BLiSS): 1.5M naturalistic minimal pairs derived from errorful sentence–correction pairs in parallel learner corpora. We use them to evaluate L2LMs trained under different regimes on specific properties of learner language, giving a linguistically motivated, controlled measure of interlanguage competence.

publications.title: What's the Best Sequence Length for BabyLM?
publications.venue: BabyLM Workshop, EMNLP 2025 · Suzhou, China
publications.finding: For BabyLM pretraining, longer context often helps but not always: short sequences suffice for grammar tasks, while morphological reasoning benefits from longer ones.
publications.takeaway: There is no single best context length; it depends on the task.
publications.summary: Transformer language models use a fixed context window that has grown in step with pretraining dataset size, yet many BabyLM submissions default to much shorter sequences. We ask a simple question: what sequence length should we use when training BabyLMs? Using 100M words of training data and fixed compute budgets, we compare 125M-parameter Mamba and OPT models. Longer is often better, but the best length depends on both task and architecture. Shorter sequences are enough for grammatical generalization, while longer contexts help morphological analogical reasoning.

publications.title: Extended Abstract for “Linguistic Universals": Emergent Shared Features in Independent Monolingual Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
publications.venue: 5th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL), EMNLP 2025 · Suzhou, China
publications.finding: Aligns sparse-autoencoder features across separately trained monolingual models to look for universal features that emerge independently.
publications.takeaway: Languages may share structure that models rediscover on their own.
publications.summary: Do independently trained monolingual language models converge on shared linguistic principles? We analyse a suite of models trained separately on single languages with identical architectures and budgets. We train sparse autoencoders on their activations to get interpretable latent features, then align those features across languages using activation correlations. Pairwise analyses test whether the feature spaces converge in non-trivial ways, and we look for universal features that recur across models.
